A vast irrigation scheme on the plain between the Blue Nile and the White Nile south of Khartoum, in Sudan. Water began to flow in 1925, when the Sennar Dam on the Blue Nile was finished. It became one of the largest irrigation projects in the world under a single management.

It was built under the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan to grow long-staple cotton for the mills of Lancashire, the industry born in the cotton revolution. A British company ran it, the government provided the water, and Sudanese tenant farmers grew the cotton, each side taking a share of the profit. Tenants also grew food crops on their plots.

Cotton from Gezira paid for much of the colonial state and later of independent Sudan. The scheme was nationalised in 1950 and later enlarged. From the 1970s it declined, with silted canals, falling yields and debts. The French built a similar scheme on the Niger, the Office du Niger.
